scenes.title: Introduction to Growth
scenes.visual: A title text reading 'Big-O Notation' appears at the top. Below it, three functions are displayed in a vertical list: 'O(n)', 'O(n log n)', and 'O(n^2)'. Each equation glows one by one with distinct colors (Blue for n, Green for n log n, and Red for n^2).
scenes.narration: In computer science, Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's runtime scales as the input size grows. Let's compare three common time complexities: linear, n log n, and quadratic.

scenes.title: Plotting the Curves
scenes.visual: A 2D coordinate plane appears with labeled axes: horizontal axis labeled 'Input Size (n)' and vertical axis labeled 'Operations'. Three colored curves trace out smoothly from the origin: a linear line y = x in blue, a y = x log(x) curve in green, and a steep parabola y = x^2 in red. Text labels appear next to each curve.
scenes.narration: For small values of n, the difference between these algorithms might seem modest. But as n increases, their growth trajectories diverge dramatically.

scenes.title: Scaling Up to Large Inputs
scenes.visual: The camera zooms out on the coordinate plane, causing the axes to rescale to much larger numbers. The red n^2 curve shoots rapidly off the top of the frame, while the blue line stays moderate and the green n log n curve grows only slightly faster than the line. An arrow highlights the huge vertical gap between n log n and n^2.
scenes.narration: When n becomes very large, higher-order terms dominate completely. The quadratic algorithm quickly becomes impractical, while n log n scales remarkably well.

scenes.title: Dominant Term Takeaway
scenes.visual: The graph fades away leaving a large equation: 'T(n) = 3n^2 + 50n + 100'. A red rectangle highlights '3n^2'. The smaller terms '50n + 100' fade out and transform into an arrow pointing to the final simplified notation: 'O(n^2)'.
scenes.narration: That's why Big-O focuses only on the dominant term. We drop constants and lower-order terms to capture the essential rate of growth.
